newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish government clears new securities law.
newsitem.headline: Polish government clears new securities law.

text.p: The Polish government on Tuesday approved a draft law liberalising securities trading rules and making them more compatible with the capital market's development, the government's spokeswoman said.
Aleksandra Jakubowska told reporters that the full cabinet approved the draft following a recommendation by the government's economic council.

The chairman of the Polish Securities Commission (KPW), Jacek Socha, said in July that the bill, which must clear parliament, was partly aimed to adjust the law to requirements of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which Poland joined in mid-July.
The bill, largely drafted by the KPW, creates a legal framework for introducing such instruments as futures, options and other derivatives to Poland's increasingly mature stock market.
The bill would allow Polish companies to float up to 25 percent of shares abroad without the securities commission's permission, either directly or through depositary receipts.
After the year 2000, Polish companies would be allowed to float unlimited stock abroad without a permit.

Under the draft, companies traded publicly for more than 36 months would no longer be required to submit issue prospectuses of new share issues for securities commission approval, in a move to simplify the process of raising capital.
The bill would also allow foreign brokerages to open branches in Poland rather than register separate firms, as is currently the case.
The law is to be accompanied by a draft on investment funds which has yet to clear the government.
